title: 3 ways heat pumps save you money
summary: Rewiring America's page on heat pump savings from IRA rebates, the 25C tax credit and lower energy bills.

assertions.quote: The rebate’s upfront discounts will cover up to 100 percent of point-of-sale purchases for low-income households

verdicts.note: HEAR allows up to 100% of cost capped at $8,000 for low-income households, but availability depends on each state's program.

IRA electrification rebates offer up to $8,000 per low-income household (plus wiring and duct allowances), against mean heat pump upfront costs of $9,000-$24,000 in cold climates; most of the cost only for cheaper installs.

Under the federal HEAR design, rebates could cover 100% of project costs up to $14,000 per unit, with up to $8,000 for a space-heating heat pump, for low- to moderate-income households; availability depends on each state's launch, and since mid-2026 fuel-switching no longer qualifies.

assertions.quote: Your household can receive a 30 percent tax credit each year (up to $2,000) to buy and install heat pumps
The average homeowner will save $370 per year by upgrading to a heat pump.
systems that run on fuel oil, propane, or traditional electric resistance (like baseboard heat or electric furnaces) will save closer to $1,000 per year
Heat pumps cost more upfront (average heat pump installation is $16,000)
with their energy bill savings, a heat pump will often pay off in about 15 years
plus utility bill savings and lower maintenance costs
